items.text: SEASON 10 · EPISODE 5 · DRAFT · CASE-054  Coldframe Sound, the tape and drive store · week three · Maya, Hollis, Esme, Corbin and Pim · Level L6 · Mastery support (reference only — choose the tool and say why)  Ten years ago Esme made her first album in this building. The label wants its multitracks back for a reissue. The building has thirty years of sessions and no idea which of them still open.  ⚑ RV-176, RV-179: reissue rights are the label’s to clear; the performances are the artists’. RV-177: figures illustrative. Some choices run on a clock — and some depend on your loadout.

items.title: The Archive
items.stakes: The label wants Esme's first album's multitracks for a reissue — and nothing from 2016 will open.
items.clock: By the first of the month.
items.reward: An album anyone can open in ten years, and an honest list of what's gone.
items.rumor: A recording you can't open is a recording you don't have.

items.alt: The tape and drive store: shelves of tape boxes and hard drives in cases; Hollis gestures at all of it; Maya, amused.

bubbles.text: Low Country. It's all here. Somewhere. On something.
Then nobody opens anything until it's copied.

items.caption: Thirty years on the shelves.

items.prompt: 10:20. The 2016 drive spins; its partner doesn't. The session files belong to a retired program. First move?
items.risk: Damaging the only copy — or giving up on an album that's still there.
timeout: Pim opens the old session to have a look.

hints.text: What could opening an old session do to the drive it's on?

options.label: Open the sessions on the old computer and start exporting from the original drive
options.result: The program rebuilds its database — onto the only copy.
options.consequence: Writes to the thing you're trying to save.

options.label: Before opening anything, copy both drives read-only, record a checksum for every file, and work only on the copies
options.result: Drive A images cleanly. Drive B won't spin. Every file on the copy has a fingerprint.
options.consequence: Protect what exists, and prove what you started with.

options.label: Send the dead drive to a recovery lab straight away
options.result: A large bill before anyone checks what the DVDs hold.
options.consequence: Maybe later — after you know what's missing.

options.label: Tell Corbin the multitracks are lost
options.result: Corbin cancels the reissue. On Wednesday the DVDs turn up.

items.title: Twenty-four tracks, fifteen here.
items.body: On the copies, every song's session expects 24 tracks. Only 15 are on drive A; the other 9 lived on the scratch drive that won't spin. In a box behind the door: two sets of DVDs from 2016. From them, 96 of the 99 missing files come back. Three won't read — a tambourine and two backing-vocal passes.
items.label: Test: how much is lost — and how big was the hole?

items.alt: A status sheet for Low Country (2016): session files won't open; drive A spins with 15 of 24 tracks per song; the scratch drive won't spin; two DVD sets, FINAL and FINAL 2, disagree; 96 of 99 files recovered and 3 unreadable; no checksums anywhere; pencil track sheets in the tape box.
items.caption: The hole, measured.

items.title: pencil · ‘LC · FINAL = comp B’
items.body: Inside the Low Country tape box, under the lid: Hollis's pencil track sheets for all eleven songs, and on the last page, ‘FINAL = comp B. FINAL 2 = Esme's alt — NOT released.’ The only metadata that survived was a pencil.

items.title: The new book that couldn't be read
items.body: In 1986, to mark nine hundred years since the Domesday Book, the British public broadcaster gathered a new survey of the country onto two interactive laser discs, readable only with a special player and computer. Within about fifteen years almost nothing could read them, and rescuing the contents took a dedicated project. The nine-hundred-year-old original was still on its shelf, legible.

items.title: FINAL and FINAL 2.
items.body: The two DVD sets aren't the same. Several vocal files differ in length; nothing records which set was released, and there are no checksums to compare against. Hollis finds his pencil track sheets under the tape box lid: ‘FINAL = comp B. FINAL 2 = Esme's alt — NOT released.’ Esme listens to both and hears the line she changed on the last night. FINAL it is.
items.label: Test: what would have settled it in a minute — and whose call are the lost parts?

items.alt: The store; Esme with headphones round her neck, smiling; Hollis holding a yellowed track sheet.

bubbles.text: That one. I changed ‘river’ to ‘rain’ on the last night.
And I wrote it down. In pencil. Ten years ago.

items.prompt: I changed that line on the last night. I'd forgotten until I heard it.

options.label: “Then you just did what no checksum could — you told us which one was real.”
options.reply: Low Country's still in there, then. Good.

options.label: “It would've been easier with notes.”
options.reply: I was twenty-four. I didn't take notes. I took the train home.

items.prompt: FINAL is the released version. Three parts are lost. What goes to the label?
unknown: What Esme wants for the lost parts
items.risk: The wrong version reissued — or a quiet fake in a piece of history.
timeout: Both sets sit on the table; Corbin's deadline moves closer.

hints.text: What do you know, what don't you, and who decides the rest?

options.label: Deliver FINAL 2 — it has the newer date
options.result: The reissue would have carried the take Esme rejected.

options.label: Deliver FINAL, confirmed by the track sheets and Esme; list the three lost parts plainly; Esme decides whether they're re-recorded; Corbin clears the rights before anything goes to a remixer
options.result: Corbin gets 261 files and a one-page list of what's gone. Esme decides to re-record the tambourine herself and leave the two harmonies out.
options.consequence: The truth about what exists, and each decision with its owner.

options.label: Send both sets to the remixer and let them choose
options.result: The remixer now has an unreleased version of her song.
options.consequence: Unreleased performances out of the building without consent.
options.fail: Unreleased performances don't leave without the artist's say-so.

options.label: Rebuild the three lost parts from the stereo mix with separation software, and don't mention it
options.result: Nobody would notice — until someone did.
options.consequence: Passing off a reconstruction as the original.
options.fail: Quietly replacing lost parts misrepresents the artist's recording.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #96 · AVERY'S LENS  Archive for the person who opens it in ten years  A session only survives if someone who wasn't there can open it: plain formats, the paperwork beside the audio, proof every copy is intact — and a date to check again.  Ten years on, the session files wouldn't open, a third of the tracks were on a dead drive, and two ‘final’ backups disagreed. A pencil track sheet decided it.

items.alt: The status sheet after the rescue: session files kept but not relied on; every track exported as Broadcast WAV from bar 1, the same length; 261 of 264 tracks exported; 96 of 99 recovered and 3 lost, listed; FINAL confirmed by the track sheets and Esme; a checksum manifest of 261 files; three copies, one off-site, a yearly fixity check.
items.caption: Openable by someone who wasn't there.

items.title: ‘licence server closed’
items.body: A printout pinned in the store: the recording program's maker announcing, years ago, that its licence server would close and the old version would stop opening. Somebody had pinned it. Nobody had acted on it.

items.prompt: Low Country is safe. What keeps the next thirty years of sessions openable?
items.risk: The next reissue request, and thirty years of unopenable sessions.
timeout: The shelves stay as they are.

hints.text: Who will open these files in ten years — and what will they need?

options.label: Archive the session files — they hold everything

A preservation standard in the studio runbook, owned by Pim: Broadcast WAV exports from bar 1, scanned track sheets and a readme, a checksum manifest, three copies with one off-site, a yearly fixity check and a five-year migration
options.result: Pim writes it up and books the first fixity check. Hollis starts on the 1996 shelf.
options.consequence: Written down, owned, and on the calendar.

options.label: Do this album properly; write the process up ‘when there's time’
options.result: Low Country is safe. The next album goes on the shelf the old way.
options.consequence: The best you can do without a runbook — and it saves one album.

options.label: Keep the old computer in a cupboard so the sessions can always be opened
options.result: It won't start in five years.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  A session file is instructions, not audio. Archive for the person who opens it in ten years: copy read-only and checksum first; list what each session expects; recover and log every failure; settle conflicts with paperwork and the people who were there; export every track as Broadcast WAV from bar 1; keep a readme, a manifest and three copies; book the next fixity check. Say plainly what’s lost — the artist decides what happens to it.
REFLECTION (optional)  · What of yours would be unreadable if the program that made it disappeared tomorrow?
